issues.description: HAS_TIME regex is an unannotated over-approximation that reads like a validator.
issues.detail: The `/\dm?s/i` guard is a cheap pre-filter, not a parser: it matches non-time substrings inside identifiers, URLs, or custom props (e.g. `url(a1s.png)`, `1ms-foo`). That's acceptable because valueParser still does the authoritative work, but the intent should be named. Add a one-line comment stating it is a fast over-approximation with exactness delegated to valueParser, or extract a `mayContainTime(value)` predicate.

issues.description: Performance claim ships with no benchmark or measurement.
issues.detail: The PR title is "Fix performance" but neither the changeset nor the diff contains before/after numbers, a profile, or a microbenchmark. walkDecls runs on every declaration, so the fast-path is plausibly hot, but as written this is asserted, not proved. Attach timings or cite the profile from #6869 so the baseline is recorded and future regressions are detectable.

issues.description: No test locks in that the short-circuit actually skips valueParser.
issues.detail: Existing rule tests still pass by reading, but nothing asserts that declarations without time-shaped values bypass the parser. A targeted unit test (or spy) would prevent a future refactor from silently moving the parse above the guard and undoing the optimization without anyone noticing.

synthesis.summary: Panel consensus: ACCEPT with nits. The patch is small, well-shaped, and correct in spirit — a cheap regex pre-filter that short-circuits walkDecls before the expensive valueParser call, with the authoritative parsing still running on candidates. Main concerns are about evidence and clarity rather than correctness: the HAS_TIME regex is an unannotated over-approximation that should be named or commented, and the "fix performance" claim ships without any benchmark numbers to anchor the baseline. A test that pins the short-circuit behavior would harden the optimization against future drift.
